newsitem.title: USA: Dlr drop won't affect U.S. inflation much--Ehrlich.
newsitem.headline: Dlr drop won't affect U.S. inflation much--Ehrlich.

text.p: A senior Clinton administration official on Wednesday played down the inflationary impact of the recent decline of the dollar.

"I don't think, on a trade weighted basis, the rollback or the decline of the dollar of the last several days and weeks is enough to materially change the (inflation) situation," Commerce Undersecretary Everett Ehrlich said.
He told Reuters Financial Television that prices of goods imported into the United States have been relatively restrained recently, thanks in part to lower prices for oil.
The government reported earlier that U.S. import prices fell 0.9 percent in April after a 1.2 percent fall in March.

The dollar has dropped some 10 percent against the Japanese yen this month. Ehrlich attributed the decline to changing expectations in financial markets about the outlook for U.S. and Japanese interest rates.

"The dollar seems to be falling back vis-a-vis the yen because there are expectations that rates are not going to rise dramatically in the United States while they might rise in the future in Japan," he said.

Ehrlich said the past strength of the dollar against the yen may have a lingering effect on U.S. trade with Japan in the coming months. But he argued that structural and macroeconomic factors were, and would be, more important.
The government reported earlier that the U.S. trade deficit with Japan rose by more than eight percent in April. But the global U.S. deficit fell, by more than 19 percent.

Based on the trade and other recent data, Ehrlich said the U.S. economy looks to have grown by nearly six percent in the first quarter. He said his "personal guess" is that growth will slow to around three percent in the current quarter.
